full_judgment:
4. The allegations made in the plaint giving rise to the cause of action for the instant, suit have been stated in a lengthy plaint running over 44 paragraphs. We shall briefly state the plaintiff's case in the following term:- The suit land is the foreshore char land on the western bank of river Barisal known as Kirtonkhola which is a public navigable river. The Barisal bi-weekly market within the Municipality of Barisal situated in Mouza Amanatganj is adjacent to the west of the suit land. According to the plaintiff, Baisharashi Chowdhyrashi landlords of Bauphal Estate as they are popularly known were the owners in possession of the bi-weekly market. The plaintiff's specific case is that the disputed foreshore land is a char land which was under Kirtonkhola river and gradually appeared as an accretion to the hat since 1950. At that time part of the char was above water level and parts thereof were in process of formation. With the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act coming into operation, the interests of the landlords of Bauphal Estate were acquired and the plaintiff took possession of the aforesaid bi-weekly market. With the formation of the char land certain persons claimed interest in the foreshore land as an accretion to their karsha interest on the basis of settlement from the Bauphal Estate. The Government, however, did not recognise those persons in unauthorised occupation and after hearing their claims recognised only those who had valid settlement and rejected the claims of others. The Government while in khas possession of the foreshore char land by granting licences for construction of jetty, certain persons stealthily entered into the suit land and made certain unauthorised constructions. At the relevant time the char lands were gill soft and unfit for cultivation, The Government took notice of the possession of these unauthorised persons and served notice from them -in Miscellaneous case No. 18.S/55-56 under Act X of 1953 Government lands and Building (Recovery) Act. Thereafter defendant No. 1 Syed Hatem Ali put up certain unauthorised constructions which were also demolished and removed on 16-7-57. Meanwhile defendant No. 1 some how managed to get his name recorded in the S. A. khation but the entry in the record of right was struck off at the instance of the Government and record stood in the name of the Government. Defendant No. 1 Syed Hatem Ali moved the Dacca High Court in Writ petition challenging the legality of the notice under Act X of 1953. The High Court after hearing the matter allowed the petition and made the Rule absolute restraining the Government by an appropriate injunction from interfering with the possession of the defendant. This decision of the High Court gave rise to the cause of action for this suit. The plaintiff claims the suit land as foreshore land of river Barisal known as Kitton khola and also as an accretion arising from the river bed which belonged to the Government in a proprietary right as appertaining to Mouza Char Badna. The other basis of the plaintiff's claim appears on the basis of acquisition under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of the interest of the Bauphal Estate landlords in the market situated in Mouza Anmatganj. It further appears that as an alternative case was sought to be spelt out that the suit land being adjunct to the bi-weekly hat, the Government acquired the same. For the purpose of establishing the claim over the suitland the plaintiff claimed that the bed of Kirton Khola river belonged to the Government, The plaintiff however, denied the claim of the defendants of the alleged settlement on the basis of Amaldari from Bauphal Estate and of possession therein. It is the consistent case of the plaintiff as available from the schedule to the plaint that the suit land appertains to Mouza Char Badna and not Amanatganj. 

 20. The other case of the plaintiff is that the suit land being the khas land of the Bauphal land lords with accretion to their permanently settled estate and appertaining to mouza Amanatganj, having been acquired under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the Government acquired title. While considering this case of the plaintiff, it is necessary to remember that the plaintiff is to succeed on the strength and proof of its own case and not on the weakness of the defence case. The learned Additional Attorney General repeatedly argued before us that the defendants having failed to prove their title to the suit land, the plaintiff has acquired good title. Such a proposition appears to be a clear departure from the established principles of law. The plaintiff is required to prove its case to the hilt. The plaintiff in this behalf appears to be shaky and could not spell out a definite and defined case. We are not oblivious of the principle that in the cases where char land is involved, the pleadings is not to be construed too strictly. Giving that allowance to the plaintiff, let us consider the case of acquisition of the suit land as excess khas land of the outgoing land-lords by the Government. Mr. Pal appears to have correctly pointed out that the proceedings in Exhibits 3(b) and 3(d) do not conclusively indicate that the suit land was acquired according to law and in terms of section 20 of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act. We are, however, not directly concerned with the alleged title of the defendants based on their claim of settlement on the basis of an Amaldari and on payment of rent in terms thereof. In this suit, in our opinion, there is hardly any scope for determination of defendant's title. We are mainly concerned with the claim of the plaintiff as alleged in the plaint and sought to be proved in evidence. On scrutiny of the evidence, it appears that the witnesses fumbled to speak out any date or year when the suit land re-appeared. It is necessary to remember that the plaintiff's claim is that the suit land re-appeared after 1950. There is a significant gap between 1950 and 1954 when the Bauphal Estate was acquired by a notification under section 3(1) and 3(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Unless it is shown that the suit land re-appeared before the Acquisition in 1954, the claim of the plaintiff that the suit land vested as excess khas land of Bauphal landlords cannot stand. It will have to be examined whether the suit land was the khas land of the landlords and in excess of the retainable quantity. The plain-tiff is also in a vacillating mood here. On this point no issue has been raised although this is one of the grounds of plaintiff's claim. No evidence of conclusive nature was adduced by the plaintiff to show that the suit land re-re-appeared in Amanatganj before Bauphal Estate was acquired. There is also no definite evidence to show that it was an accretion to the biweekly market. It is necessary to observe that different consequences will follow if either of the alternatives is proved, namely the suit land appertaining to mouza Amanatganj and belonging to permanently settled estate of the Bauphal Landlords if re-appeared before the acquisition under section 3 of the Act, in that case, the Government may acquire title upon a proper proceeding under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act upon proof that the same was excess khas land of the ex-proprietors. In the other case, if it is an accretion to the hat before the acquisition under section 3 of the Act, the Government cannot claim the suit land as an adjunct or .appendix to the hat. We have been taken through certain maps and also the oral evidence of the P.Ws. It is apparent that the hat and the suit land are intervened by strips of land which have been described as Chandina and in occupation of certain tenants evidently on the basis of settlement from the Bauphal Estate and recognized as tenants by the Government under the. State Acquisition and Tenancy Act The evidence on record does not indicate that the suit land is an accretion to hat. Therefore, these two contentions have to be kept in isolation and the plaintiff is required to prove its case relating to acquisition of title to the suit land as has been claimed by it. An accretion to the hat does not automatically vest in the Government within the meaning and scope of section 20 of the Act, if such accretion took place before the notification under section 3 of the said Act. Section 20 does not speak of acquisition of land adjunct or accretion to the hat. In the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, section 20 has clearly illustrated the nature of non-retainable land. Only those classes of non-retainable lands vest in the Government in the terms of section 20. Section 20 also prescribes the limit of retainable land. Therefore, there is no ground to conceive that an adjunct to a hat stood acquired with the hat under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. We are therefore, left with the only other conceivable case of the Government that the suitland was the excess khas land of the Bauphal Estate. In this regard, as it appears, due consideration should made as to when the land in suit re-appeared in situ. As painted out earlier, there is no conclusive evidence nor there is any clear indication in the Plaint and evidence as to the time when this land reappeared in view of the nitrate azalea we propose to make in this a appeal, we need not say anything more at this stage on the merit of the plaintiff's case in this regard. We have taken sufficient precaution in expressing our views on the questions which may require fur there considerate ion by the trial court.
